tag: Episode 27 Side Story · The One Who Stays
title: The One Who Stays

beats.t: The night before the door opened. All the bakery lights were out, and only the oven breathed low.
Yundal sat alone on a chair before it. A yellow sheet and a brush rested on his knees. Three layers of bandages covered the hole that had spread to his wrist.
All right, dear customer. Last service of the day.
There was no customer. Yundal was used to talking to himself. Since people had begun forgetting him, half his conversations had always been with himself.
The brush passed over the paper. 乙亥. His lady's Day Pillar. Eight small stars around it. He left the last star empty.
A talisman is strongest when used only once. Try to use it twice, and greed gets into it.
He held the finished talisman to the firelight, then nodded in satisfaction.
Wayfinding Talisman. Once, it lights our lady's way back. No expiry date. No refunds.
What are you doing there?
Oh, Mr. Cat. Customer Support patrols at night, too.
I followed the smell. Ink.
Neo looked at the talisman in Yundal's hand. Then the bandage beneath it. A black stain seeped from its edge.
Is that for Yeoni?
Yes. I'll slip it into her bread bag tomorrow. Give it directly, and she'll thank me. Then I think I'll cry again.
You don't cry.
You don't know me at all, Mr. Cat. I cry easily. People just forget that I did.
Neo did not answer. Instead, he sat in the chair beside Yundal. For a while, they watched the oven fire together.
You knew you couldn't cross the door?
Yes. Since I first fell into this world. Without your birth hour, you can't return. I've reached that door twice in three years.
Both times...
Yes. Both times, the door failed to recognize me.
A log collapsed in the oven. Sparks flew. Yundal caught one in his bandaged hand. It vanished into the hole in his palm.
I'll stay beside Yeoni over there. You hold on here.
Of course. Holding on is the one thing I'm good at.
And... thank you. For today, at the river.
Wow. Mr. Cat said thank you. Write that on a talisman and sell it, and I'd make a fortune.
I take it back.
The following morning, the door opened. Golden wind filled the bakery storeroom.
As his lady crossed the threshold, Yundal murmured a name very softly. A name other than Yundal. Hoping the person crossing might take it along.
The wind covered it. His lady seemed to glance back. But the door was already closing.
Too much to hope for, then.
The door became an old storage door again. It ended more quickly than he'd expected. Yundal stood there a long time, then stroked the handle once. Still warm.
Around noon, Moka packed. His luggage amounted to a bundle of metal skewers.
Then I'm off. Festival island. Need to catch a boat before sunset.
Take care, Mr. Otter. Cut back on the rapping, too.
Not cutting back on rap. And don't mope alone, con artist. If you're going to mope, come do it on the festival island. I'll give you skewers.
Free?
On credit.
With that, Moka ran toward the dock. Not once did he turn. So Yundal could keep waving until the otter's tail vanished at the alley's end.
That night, Yundal unfolded a sheet at a table in the bakery corner. Not a talisman this time. Just white paper.
He dipped his brush in ink and wrote a name. Not Yundal. The name he had always written beneath his home address three years ago.
Before the ink dried, the letters' edges blurred. Stroke by stroke, they erased themselves, as though sinking into the paper. When the last vanished, the sheet was white again.
A little fast today.
He wrote again. It vanished again. The third time, he put down the brush and read the name aloud.
The name dispersed in the air the moment it became sound. Among bread smells and oven smoke. Reaching nobody's ears.
It's all right. I remember.
He didn't know whether it really was all right. But over three years, he had learned very well how to say it.
Mister, aren't you sleeping?
Ah, Miss Luna. You're awake?
Thirsty. Mister, what's your name? My sister said to ask in the morning. You're a first-time customer who keeps staying.
Yundal's face froze briefly. A first-time customer. Not words to hear from someone who had baked bread beside him yesterday.
Yundal. Leap month. A month that's there, yet isn't. So it's a name you don't have to feel bad about forgetting.
Mr. Yundal. I've memorized it! I'll tell Sis tomorrow.
Thank you. Then please ask me again tomorrow.
Yawning, Luna returned to her room. Yundal watched her for a long time. Tomorrow morning, that child would ask again. Mister, what's your name?
Yundal opened the bakery door and stepped into the alley. He looked up. The fissure where Black Moon had been driven away was closed. But not completely.
Starlight seeped through the sealed crack. Not this world's stars. Unfamiliar stars in twelve rows, one great unnamed star set in each.
Another sky.
The hole in his palm pulled toward that starlight on its own. As it always had since appearing. Toward Black Moon.
There you are. The master of the thing that ate my time.
Yundal adjusted his glove, firmly over the bandages.
Our lady will return if she uses the talisman. That's the kind of person she is. Someone who can't forget the taste of bread.
Then I'll go ahead and secure a place. Location matters for a compatibility booth.
Mr. Cat will get jealous again. That helps business, too.
The next morning, when Luna's sister opened the bakery, nobody sat at the corner table. One brush and one white sheet. Nothing was written on it.
Who left paper here?
Luna's sister folded it and put it in a drawer. She did not throw it away. She didn't know why, either.
